title: From generation to generation
hook: the phrase that ends the Kedushah

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hatikvah, and your line: the hope. Today, a phrase the synagogue sings to keep hope and memory moving.

Partway through a weekday service, the leader repeats the standing prayer, the Amidah, out loud, and the room changes. Leader and congregation start trading lines from the Bible, back and forth, a call and an answer. Some people rise up onto their toes. First comes Isaiah's vision of the angels: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts". Then Ezekiel's: blessed be the glory of the LORD from His place. Then a verse from the Psalms. And just before the closing hallelujah, the congregation sings today's word.
screen: `THE AMIDAH, REPEATED ALOUD.` → `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.` → `JUST BEFORE HALLELUJAH.`

segments.voice: L'dor vador. Dor means generation. L'dor, to a generation; vador, and a generation: from generation to generation. That section of the service is the Kedushah, the prayer of holiness, and its last verse is from Psalm 146: the LORD will reign for ever, your God, O Zion, l'dor vador, hallelujah. Then, in the Ashkenazi wording, the leader picks the phrase straight back up: l'dor vador nagid godlecha, from generation to generation we will tell of your greatness. Look at the shape of it. Isaiah's angels call holy in heaven. Ezekiel hears the glory moving from its place. Then the prayer comes down to earth and lands on something very human: parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren. Holiness here isn't only sung. It's handed down. The phrase has roots in the Torah too. At the burning bush, God gives Moses a name and says, "this is My memorial unto all generations", in Hebrew, l'dor dor. A memorial keeps memory alive, so the zachor of a few days ago and today's phrase belong together: remembering is how anything gets from one generation to another. And the Kedushah is a conversation. The congregation answers the leader; the leader answers the congregation. Passing something on works like that too. The young don't only receive. They answer back, with questions and new melodies of their own, and the answer becomes part of what the next generation hears.
screen: `DOR: A GENERATION.` · `THE KEDUSHAH ENDS: L'DOR VADOR.` · `THIS IS MY MEMORIAL UNTO ALL GENERATIONS.` · `A CALL, AND AN ANSWER.` · then, large: `GENERATION TO GENERATION.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone younger than you, a child, a niece or nephew, a student, a new coworker, a neighbor's kid, and hold their face for a moment. Ask two things: what do I know that they might need someday, and what do they know that I don't? If you pray, say the psalm's two words quietly, l'dor vador; if you don't, just hold their name.
L'dor vador. From generation to generation: the words near the end of the Kedushah, from Psalm 146. Today's word.
Your line: generation to generation. A call, an answer, and then the next voice. That's day one thousand fifty-nine.

howItsDone: When a minyan is present, the leader repeats the Amidah aloud and the congregation joins in the Kedushah, standing; in the Ashkenazi wording the leader then continues with l'dor vador nagid godlecha.

chat.says: What does l'dor vador mean? I keep seeing it on family keepsakes.
options: From generation to generation; it's sung near the end of the Kedushah.
It means holy, holy, holy, the angels' words in the prayer.
It's a toast for good luck at weddings and family parties.
chat.meaning: Dor means generation. The words come from Psalm 146, sung just before the Kedushah's closing hallelujah.

Amidah.meaning: the standing prayer, the heart of each Jewish service

Kedushah.meaning: the prayer of holiness, sung when the Amidah is repeated aloud

nagid godlecha.meaning: Hebrew: we will tell of your greatness

Ashkenazi.meaning: of the Jews of Central and Eastern European roots

sources.ref: Kedushah of the Amidah repetition, with 'l'dor vador nagid godlecha' (Ashkenazi rite)

notes: Kedushah described as said in the leader's repetition of the Amidah, with Isaiah 6:3, Ezekiel 3:12 and Psalm 146:10; 'l'dor vador nagid godlecha' attributed to the Ashkenazi wording only (Sephardi and other rites continue differently). Please confirm.
'Some people rise up onto their toes' at kadosh: custom, softened with 'some'.
Psalm 146:10 and Ezekiel 3:12 paraphrased (not quoted) because the exact JPS 1917 wording was not certain; Isaiah 6:3 and Exodus 3:15 quoted from JPS 1917. Please confirm both quotations.
Exodus 3:15 Hebrew 'zichri l'dor dor' glossed as l'dor dor; please confirm.
Hook says 'a weekday service'; the Kedushah is also said on Shabbat with different wording. Please confirm this is acceptable.
